item.title: Consensus on a core outcome set for ventilation trials in critically ill patients with acute brain injury: results of an international Delphi consensus study
item.description:
Purpose: Clinical research evaluating mechanical ventilation liberation in patients with acute brain injury (ABI) shows substantial outcome heterogeneity, limiting evidence synthesis. We aimed to develop an internationally endorsed core outcome set (COS) and a hierarchical composite endpoint for ventilation trials in neurocritical care.

Methods: Following COS-STAD/COS-STAP standards, we conducted a 4-round international Delphi study. Candidate outcomes were identified via a scoping review. A multidisciplinary panel from 31 countries scored outcomes using a 9-point GRADE scale. Inclusion required >70% rating as "critical" (score 7-9) and ≤15% as "not important" (1-3). Two consensus meetings were held to categorize outcomes, select representative measures, and ratify a hierarchical composite endpoint.

Results: 78 stakeholders participated in Round 1; 60 completed all rounds (23.1% attrition). Fifty-four outcomes achieved Delphi consensus. At Consensus Meeting 1, these were organized into 16 categories; the highest-scoring outcome per category was selected. Three outcomes were not ratified due to disease-specificity (NIH Stroke Scale) or lack of universal applicability (brain death, coma-free days). The final COS comprised 13 outcomes across 5 domains: respiratory function, survival, complications, functional status, and quality of life. A 3-level hierarchical composite endpoint was ratified at Consensus Meeting 2: (1) intensive care unit survival, (2) no reintubation within 72 hours, and (3) days alive without mechanical ventilation.

Conclusion: This study establishes the first COS for ventilation weaning trials in ABI patients. Widespread adoption of these 13 outcomes and the hierarchical composite endpoint will standardize reporting, enable meaningful evidence synthesis, and facilitate clinical translation in neurocritical care.

Trial registration: Core Outcome Measures in Effectiveness Trials (COMET) Initiative, registration number 2320.

Fong N, Burns G, Phillips J, Digitale J, Ghasemian A, Cinotti R

item.title: Individualized treatment effects of high flow nasal oxygen in immunocompromised patients
item.description:
Rationale: High flow nasal oxygen (HFNO) has become a common first-line practice for acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (ARF). In immunocompromised patients, ARF is the leading cause of ICU admission, yet a randomized trial found no overall benefit of HFNO in this population.

Objectives: To assess whether baseline characteristics influence HFNO's effectiveness in preventing invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) in immunocompromised patients with ARF.

Methods: A causal forest machine-learning algorithm was derived in the HIGH trial (776 patients randomized to HFNO or conventional oxygen) to predict the HFNO effects on day-28 IMV incidence. Patients with a "do-not-intubate" order (n = 72) were excluded. Model performance was validated through 500 bootstrap iterations and patients were categorized into terciles based on predicted HFNO benefit. Transportability of the model was assessed in an independent observational cohort (818 patients).

Main results: Among the 704 participants, HFNO's average effect on day-28 IMV was not significant. However, substantial heterogeneity in treatment responses was identified (predicted benefit: from 20.2% [IQR 15.5%-23.9%] absolute IMV risk reduction with HFNO to 7.4% risk reduction [2.9%-11.2%] with conventional oxygen). Patients with the highest predicted benefit were older, more frequently solid organ transplant recipients, less neutropenic, more severely hypoxemic/tachycardic, but with lower non-respiratory sequential organ failure assessment (SOFA) scores. In this subgroup, HFNO was associated with a significant lower incidence of IMV. In the observational cohort, the benefit-ranking performance was preserved, although absolute effect estimates were less calibrated.

Conclusions: These results suggest HFNO might benefit specific immunocompromised patients with ARF. Further prospective studies are needed to validate these findings.

Maillard A, Métais M, Lemiale V, Mokart D, Moreau AS, Canet E

item.title: Establishing curriculum priorities for intensive care recovery education: an international Delphi study
item.description:
Purpose: To effectively support recovery, intensive care unit (ICU) clinicians require training to identify patients at risk of post-intensive care syndrome and implement interventions during and after ICU admission. This study aimed to identify and prioritise curriculum topics for educating interprofessional ICU clinicians on evidence-based ICU recovery care across the continuum of critical illness.

Methods: A two-round e-Delphi study followed by a structured consensus meeting endorsed by the European Society of Intensive Care Medicine (ESICM) was conducted. A steering committee generated an initial list of curriculum topics. In round 1, participants rated topic importance (9-point Likert scale) and suggested additional topics. In round 2, they rated newly identified topics and ranked priorities. Topics reaching consensus (≥70% rating as critical [7-9]; ≤15% rating as not important [1-3]) were discussed during the final consensus meeting.

Results: Participants' mean age was 43.5 (±10.5) years and they were predominantly female (n = 90, 66.7%). Priority topics included early mobilisation during ICU admission, post-intensive care syndrome, delirium prevention and management, implementation of the ABCDEF bundle, and cognitive support and rehabilitation. The final set of learning modules for a future curriculum was established.

Conclusion: Priority topics and learning modules for an expert-developed curriculum framework for ICU recovery were established with interprofessional ICU clinicians through a structured international consensus process with moderate levels of participant retention between the two Delphi rounds and full consensus agreement among experts. This framework may support in delivering recovery-focused care across the continuum of critical illness.

van Mol M, Karner V, Akerman E, van den Boogaard M, Brooks K, Meyer J

item.title: Sodium bicarbonate therapy for metabolic acidosis in critically ill patients: a Bayesian systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
item.description:
Purpose: To evaluate the effects of sodium bicarbonate therapy on mortality and renal outcomes in critically ill adults with metabolic acidosis.

Methods: We performed a systematic review and Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing intravenous sodium bicarbonate with placebo or usual care in adult intensive care unit patients with metabolic acidosis. MEDLINE, Embase and CENTRAL were searched from inception to December 2025, with an updated search on 2 April 2026. The primary outcome was short-term all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included renal replacement therapy (RRT) initiation, 90-day mortality, RRT-free days, vasopressor-free days, intensive care unit and hospital length of stay and adverse events.

Results: Four RCTs including 1544 patients were analysed. Sodium bicarbonate did not show a clear short-term mortality benefit (RR 0.94, 95% CrI 0.73-1.22), with a posterior probability of benefit of 72.1%. For RRT initiation, sodium bicarbonate was associated with a lower risk (RR 0.74, 95% CrI 0.59-0.98), with a posterior probability of benefit of 97.2%. Effects on other outcomes were small or imprecise, and no consistent safety signal was identified.

Conclusion: Current randomised evidence does not demonstrate a clear survival benefit from sodium bicarbonate therapy in critically ill adults with metabolic acidosis, but suggests a high probability of reducing RRT initiation. Further trials should define the patients most likely to benefit. PROSPERO registration: CRD420251246519.

Kitisin N, Walker HGM, Jung B, Jaber S, Mouncey P, Ke L
